title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation

paper.title: R u b r i c J u d g m e n t s L a c k U n c e r t a i n t y : Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier.
However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria.
Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity.
As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL).
To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW) , a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration.
Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal p p -values with provable coverage guarantees.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Evaluating open-ended outputs of large language models (LLMs) increasingly relies on rubric-based evaluation, in which response quality is decomposed into explicit criteria and assessed by LLM verifiers ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ) . Generally, the verifier renders binary pass or fail judgments on these prompt-specific criteria, which are then aggregated into a response-level score ( Cook et al., 2024 ) . The resulting scores underpin downstream applications such as ranking candidate responses ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) , providing reward signals for reinforcement learning (RL) ( Mu et al., 2024 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Shan and Shao, 2026 ) and verifying agent systems ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026c ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Xu et al., 2026d ) . Consequently, reliable aggregation of rubric judgments is essential for both LLM response evaluation and policy optimization. Despite rapid progress in rubric generation and evolution ( Cook et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , aggregation of rubric judgments heavily relies on uniform weighting. This uniformity reflects a critical limitation: rubric judgments carry no signal of uncertainty. Verifiers output a binary decision per criterion, without any confidence signal that aggregation could use for weighting. However, the difficulty of rendering a reliable judgment varies substantially across criteria ( Song et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . For example, format-level checks are typically clear-cut, while criteria involving tone, helpfulness, or content quality are often inherently subjective and harder to judge ( Pombal et al., 2026 ) . Under uniform aggregation, both types of criteria are collapsed into binary votes and given equal weight. When two responses are otherwise closely matched, an uncertain judgment on one subjective criterion can be enough to invert the overall preference. However, existing work on uncertainty quantification for LLM judges does not fully address the need for per-criterion, uncertainty-aware weighting. One line of work uses conformal prediction to estimate response-level uncertainty, either as a prediction interval over the aggregated rating ( Sheng et al., 2025 ; Liu, 2026 ) or as a confidence flag ( Wagner et al., 2024 ) , characterizing uncertainty in the final rating rather than at the criterion level. Another line of work derives confidence from decoding-time consistency, but requires non-zero-temperature sampling ( Li et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026 ) or heterogeneous verifier committees ( Fathullah and Gales, 2025 ) , both incompatible with common deterministic, single-verifier settings. A third line of work trains dedicated uncertainty modules on top of LLM judges, either by fine-tuning uncertainty-aware evaluators ( Xie et al., 2025 ) or by learning calibration probes ( Radharapu et al., 2026 ) , requiring annotated training data and producing additional output labels rather than a coverage-controlled scalar weight compatible with weighted-sum aggregation. Overall, no existing method provides a training-free, coverage-controlled, per-criterion uncertainty weight that can be applied to any binary-rubric verifier at inference time. To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW) , a training-free framework that quantifies per-criterion uncertainty of any verifier and turns it into a distribution-free aggregation weight. In the offline calibration phase, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from the verifier via a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates, and measures how well this signal aligns with gold labels on a small calibration set. In the online weighting phase, URW converts the soft signal for each new criterion into a split-conformal p p -value, which directly serves as the per-criterion aggregation weight and inherits a distribution-free guarantee: the probability of assigning a spuriously low weight to a correct judgment is provably controlled. Extensive experiments across diverse preference benchmarks and verifier families demonstrate that URW consistently improves both pairwise preference accuracy and downstream RL alignment.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: The contributions of this work are summarized as follows. ❶ We identify an overlooked limitation of rubric-based LLM evaluation: rubric judgments carry no per-criterion uncertainty, so uniform aggregation can let a single unreliable judgment on a closely contested criterion invert the overall preference between two otherwise comparable responses. ❷ We propose URW, a training-free framework for uncertainty-aware rubric weighting. URW couples paraphrase-template ensembling with split-conformal calibration, producing a per-criterion p p -value that serves as an aggregation weight and provably controls the chance of spuriously downweighting a correct judgment. ❸ We conduct comprehensive experiments on five preference benchmarks to evaluate the efficacy of URW, showing that it consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy over diverse baselines and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.

sections.heading: 2.1 Rubric-Based Preference Evaluation
sections.text: Rubric-based preference evaluation has recently emerged as an interpretable alternative or complement to conventional reward modeling ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Pan et al., 2026a ; Pan et al., 2026b ) . Specifically, given a user prompt q ∈ 𝒬 q\in\mathcal{Q} and a candidate response y ∈ 𝒴 y\in\mathcal{Y} , a rubric evaluation ( Li et al., 2025a ; Gu et al., 2026 ) decomposes the judgment into K \mathrm{K} prompt-specific binary criteria r ⁡ ( q ) = { c 1 , … , c K } r(q)=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{\mathrm{K}}\} , each phrased so that the correct answer is either 1 1 (satisfied) or 0 0 (violated). An LLM-based verifier v : 𝒬 × 𝒴 × 𝒞 → { 0 , 1 } v:\mathcal{Q}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{C}\to\{0,1\} receives each triple independently and produces a binary judgment v ⁡ ( q , y , c k ) v(q,y,c_{k}) for each criterion. Given the per-criterion verifier outputs and a scalar criterion-level weight vector 𝒘 = ( w 1 , … , w K ) \bm{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{\mathrm{K}}) with w k ≥ 0 w_{k}\geq 0 and ∑ k w k = 1 \sum_{k}w_{k}=1 , the response-level quality score of y y is obtained by weighted linear aggregation of the per-criterion judgments as follows: 𝒥 ⁡ ( y ∣ 𝒘 , q , r ) = ∑ k = 1 K w k ⋅ v ⁡ ( q , y , c k ) . \mathcal{J}\left(y\mid\bm{w},q,r\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{K}}w_{k}\cdot v(q,y,c_{k}). (1) Existing rubric-based LLM judges ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Viswanathan et al., 2026 ; Arora et al., 2025 ) typically instantiate 𝒘 \bm{w} uniformly, i.e. , w k = 1 / K w_{k}=1/\mathrm{K} , treating every criterion as equally reliable. While simple and effective, it ignores that a verifier’s per-criterion judgments vary substantially in confidence: criteria involving subjective or context-dependent quality attributes ( e.g. ,tone or helpfulness) are inherently harder to judge reliably, whereas criteria with objective, easily verifiable conditions ( e.g. ,format or length constraints) admit near-deterministic decisions. As a result, uniform aggregation treats every judgment as equally trustworthy regardless of underlying difficulty, so a single uncertain judgment carries the same influence on the aggregated score as a highly confident one.

sections.heading: 2.2 Split Conformal Prediction
sections.text: Conformal prediction ( Shafer and Vovk, 2008 ) is a general, distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification that produces prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees under mere exchangeability. Its most widely used instantiation, split conformal prediction (SCP) ( Lei et al., 2018 ) , achieves computational tractability by reserving a held-out calibration split, avoiding the need to refit the model for each test sample. Since SCP treats the underlying predictor as a black box and requires no retraining, it is naturally suited to calibrating an LLM verifier’s per-criterion certainty. Formally, let 𝒟 cal = { ( q i , y i , c i , v i ∗ ) } i = 1 N cal \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{(q_{i},y_{i},c_{i},v_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{cal}}} be a held-out calibration set of prompt-response-criterion triples with gold labels v i ∗ ∈ { 0 , 1 } v_{i}^{*}\in\{0,1\} . We assume that 𝒟 cal \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} is exchangeable with a new test triple ( q , y , c k ) (q,y,c_{k}) whose gold label v ∗ v^{*} is unknown. Given the nonconformity score s ⁡ ( q , y , c k ) = | v ⁡ ( q , y , c k ) − v ∗ | s(q,y,c_{k})=|v(q,y,c_{k})-v^{*}| , which measures the discrepancy between the verifier’s output and the gold label, and a miscoverage rate α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \alpha\in(0,1) , SCP forms the prediction set as follows: ℐ α ​ ( q , y , c k ) = { v | | v ⁡ ( q , y , c k ) − v | ≤ τ α } , τ α = Quantile ​ ( { s i } i = 1 N cal , ⌈ ( 1 − α ) ​ ( N cal + 1 ) ⌉ N cal ) , \mathcal{I}_{\alpha}(q,y,c_{k})=\big\{v\big||v(q,y,c_{k})-v|\leq\tau_{\alpha}\big\},\qquad\tau_{\alpha}=\text{Quantile}\left(\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{cal}}},\tfrac{\lceil(1-\alpha)(\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{cal}}+1)\rceil}{\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{cal}}}\right), (2) where s i = | v ⁡ ( q i , y i , c i ) − v i ∗ | s_{i}=|v(q_{i},y_{i},c_{i})-v_{i}^{*}| . Under mere exchangeability of 𝒟 cal ∪ { ( q , y , c k , v ∗ ) } \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}\cup\{(q,y,c_{k},v^{*})\} , SCP admits the finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee ℙ [ v ∗ ∈ ℐ α ( q , y , c k ) ] ≥ 1 − α \mathbb{P}\big[v^{*}\in\mathcal{I}_{\alpha}(q,y,c_{k})\big]\geq 1-\alpha .

sections.heading: 2.3 Problem Definition
sections.text: This work investigates the uncertainty-aware rubric weighting problem, specifically the challenge of constructing instance-adaptive weights w ^ k ​ ( q , y ) \hat{w}_{k}(q,y) for different rubric criteria from the outputs of a deterministic LLM verifier. These weights can be used in place of uniform weights in rubric aggregation. Ideally, they reflect the relative certainty of individual rubric judgments, so that judgments with greater uncertainty exert less influence on the response-level aggregation. However, a deterministic verifier provides only a binary judgment for each criterion and does not directly expose its certainty. Thus, the core problem is to construct w ^ k ​ ( q , y ) \hat{w}_{k}(q,y) from observable verifier behavior that captures uncertainty in individual rubric judgments.

sections.heading: 3.1 Motivation
sections.text: Judgment certainty for rubric criteria is unobservable from the LLM verifier. Each binary output v ⁡ ( q , y , c k ) v(q,y,c_{k}) carries no probability, logit, or confidence signal 1 1 1 We refer to the LLM verifier as an API-based black-box verifier. . To obtain such confidence signals, a natural solution is to sample the verifier at higher temperature. However, this departs from the deterministic decoding commonly adopted by reference verification protocols and is incompatible with downstream policy optimization algorithms that require stable reward signals. This missing uncertainty makes uniform aggregation fragile. Under w k = 1 / K w_{k}=1/\mathrm{K} , every judgment enters the aggregated score in Eq. ( 1 ) with equal influence regardless of its certainty. Consider two nearly-tied responses that agree on most criteria but are judged differently on a single subjective one ( e.g. ,tone or helpfulness): if the verifier is in fact uncertain there, that lone judgment already tips the aggregated preference, with no mechanism to discount its contribution. Case study. To substantiate the above analysis, we present an illustrative example in Figure 1 . An anxious user asks how to handle an interview: response y 1 y_{1} acknowledges the worry with warm, actionable advice, while response y 2 y_{2} gives correct steps in a curt, dismissive tone. The two responses tie on the objective criteria ( c 1 , c 2 c_{1},c_{2} ) and split the rest, so the preference hinges entirely on the empathetic-tone criterion c 5 c_{5} . Here the verifier credits the curt response y 2 y_{2} , inverting the aggregate to 𝒥 ⁡ ( y 1 ∣ q , r ) = 3 5 < 𝒥 ⁡ ( y 2 ∣ q , r ) = 4 5 \mathcal{J}(y_{1}\mid q,r)=\tfrac{3}{5}<\mathcal{J}(y_{2}\mid q,r)=\tfrac{4}{5} and contradicting the human preference y 1 ≻ y 2 y_{1}\succ y_{2} . This showcases that uniform aggregation is defenseless against a verifier’s uncertain judgments. Figure 1: A case study where a single uncertain judgment on a subjective criterion inverts the aggregated preference under uniform weighting. Some might note prior work on uncertainty quantification for LLM judges; however, its utility for rubric weighting remains under-explored. Existing methods either estimate response-wise uncertainty rather than per criterion ( Sheng et al., 2025 ; Liu, 2026 ; Wagner et al., 2024 ) , rely on higher-temperature sampling or verifier committees that depart from the deterministic reference decoding ( Li et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Fathullah and Gales, 2025 ) , or train dedicated modules that require annotated data and emit auxiliary labels instead of an criterion-level weight ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Radharapu et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, deriving a training-free, per-criterion uncertainty weight that preserves the deterministic verifier decoding remains an open and critical challenge.

sections.heading: 3.2 Quantifying Verifier Uncertainty via Template Ensembling
sections.text: In this section, we quantify a per-criterion uncertainty signal from the verifier without perturbing its decoding. The key idea is that a reliable judgment should be stable under semantics-preserving rephrasings of the criterion prompt, whereas an uncertain one flips easily. Therefore, we probe this stability with a pool of paraphrased judgment templates rather than by raising the decoding temperature. Specifically, let 𝒯 = { t 1 , … , t N } \mathcal{T}=\{t_{1},\dots,t_{\mathrm{N}}\} be a set of N \mathrm{N} judgment prompts (see Appendix C.2 for the exact pool), where each paraphrase has been checked multiple times by human experts 2 2 2 Human experts refer to our author team, who jointly reviewed and cross-checked the template pool. to confirm it preserves the original criterion’s meaning. This procedure ensures cross-template disagreement reflects verifier uncertainty rather than a shift in what is being asked. Then we apply the deterministic decoding under each template, obtaining per-template binary judgments v k , n = v ⁡ ( q , y , c k ∣ t n ) v_{k,n}=v(q,y,c_{k}\mid t_{n}) for criterion c k c_{k} . Averaging these judgments yields the soft judgment score: v ^ k := v ^ ​ ( q , y , c k ) = 1 N ​ ∑ n = 1 N v k , n ∈ { 0 , 1 N , … , 1 } , \hat{v}_{k}:=\hat{v}(q,y,c_{k})=\frac{1}{\mathrm{N}}\sum_{n=1}^{\mathrm{N}}v_{k,n}\in\left\{0,\tfrac{1}{\mathrm{N}},\dots,1\right\}, (3) which we use as the per-criterion uncertainty signal. Here v ^ k \hat{v}_{k} measures how uncertain the verifier is on the criterion: it approaches 0 0 or 1 1 when the verifier is confident and approaches 0.5 0.5 when it is maximally uncertain. Rather than thresholding the calibration scores 𝒮 \mathcal{S} at a fixed miscoverage level to form a prediction set, we measure how a test judgment ranks within 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . This rank yields a conformal p p -value ( Shafer and Vovk, 2008 ) , which grades the judgment on a continuous scale and discounts criteria on which the verifier is uncertain. sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we validate the efficacy of URW through a comprehensive empirical evaluation, centered on five research questions (RQs) as follows: 1. RQ1 : Does URW improve rubric-aggregation accuracy? In Section 4.2 , we compare URW against uncertainty-aware weighting baselines on five preference benchmarks. 2. RQ2 : Why does it work? In Section 4.3 , we perform an ablation study on the contribution of template ensembling and distribution-free calibration. 3. RQ3 : Does it generalize across verifiers and rubric sources? In Section 4.4 , we evaluate its compatibility with verifiers of varying parameter scales and with different rubric sources. 4. RQ4 : Is it sensitive to the template count? In Section 4.5 , we analyze its sensitivity to the template count N \mathrm{N} across different verifiers. 5. RQ5 : Does it improve downstream RLVR? In Section 4.6 , we use URW to aggregate the rubric rewards that drive GRPO training and evaluate the resulting policy.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. We evaluate URW on five pairwise preference benchmarks across different domains, including RubricBench ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , ResearchQA ( Yifei et al., 2026 ) , RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) , and RewardBench 2 ( Malik et al., 2026 ) . For RewardBench and RewardBench 2, we adopt their most challenging subsets, namely Chat-Hard and Precise-IF, respectively. Each benchmark supplies a response pair ( y A , y B ) (y_{\mathrm{A}},y_{\mathrm{B}}) per prompt together with a gold human preference label. For RM-Bench, whose instances list multiple chosen and rejected responses, we form pairs by diagonal matching. RubricBench and ResearchQA come with human-sourced rubrics, whereas for the remaining benchmarks we generate rubrics with RubricARM-8B-Rubric ( Xu et al., 2026c ) . For calibration in URW, we draw from the domain-diverse RUBRIC-ARROW-Judge-SFT rubric-annotation corpus ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , whose broad domain coverage supports the exchangeability our method assumes. We stratify by domain and sample 200 200 prompts, yielding about 2 2 k rubric-level annotations. The calibration set never intersects any evaluation split. Detailed dataset statistics and configurations are provided in Appendix C.1 . Baselines. We benchmark URW against a naive reference and a suite of uncertainty-aware weighting baselines, including Uniform ( w k = 1 / K w_{k}=1/\mathrm{K} ), the signal-free floor that weights all criteria equally; Beta-Binomial , a Bayesian method that treats the multi-template judgments as binomial observations under a Beta prior and derives the weight from the resulting posterior; Sampling Ensemble ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , which draws multiple high-temperature decodings per criterion and weights by their vote ratio; and SCP , a distribution-free method that calibrates the same multi-template soft score v ^ \hat{v} and hard-abstains via a global conformal quantile, together with its variant Mondrian-SCP that instead calibrates a separate quantile within each bin of v ^ \hat{v} . Implementation Details. Our main experiments employ three frozen verifiers across different model families, including DeepSeek V4 Pro ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , Qwen 3.8 Max ( Team, 2026 ) , and GLM 5.3 ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . All reference verifier calls use temperature zero, JSON mode enabled, high reasoning effort, and a maximum of 32,768 32{,}768 output tokens. The template pool contains N = 6 \mathrm{N}=6 semantics-preserving paraphrases. For the Sampling Ensemble baseline, we re-decode each rubric multiple times at temperature 0.7 0.7 . For the Beta-Binomial baseline, we place a uniform Beta ⁡ ( 1 , 1 ) \mathrm{Beta}(1,1) prior on each criterion’s satisfaction probability and take the posterior mean as the weight. Our full method uses calibrated nonconformity score set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} directly and requires no additional hyperparameter, whereas the SCP and Mondrian-SCP variants additionally use α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 and 6 6 bins. As for metrics, we report pairwise accuracy (Acc) across all benchmarks, where ties receive only half credit. More implementation details are provided in Appendix C.2 . sections.heading: 4.2 Overall Performance (RQ1)
sections.text: In this section, we compare URW with competitive baselines across five benchmarks and three verifiers. The results are presented in Table 1 with key observations as follows. ❶ Uniform aggregation yields the lowest accuracy across settings. For instance, with DeepSeek V4 Pro on ResearchQA, Uniform attains an accuracy of 0.633, whereas every uncertainty-aware weighting method attains at least 0.639. Specifically, in URW † , we retain uniform rubric weights but replace single-template criterion scores with multi-template voted scores. The variant consistently improves over Uniform aggregation baseline, with relative improvements up to 3.9% on ResearchQA. This confirms that template ensembling yields more reliable final rubric scores. ❷ Conformal uncertainty calibration is critical for rubric-weighting performance. Specifically, in URW ‡ , we retain single-template criterion scores while computing each criterion’s uncertainty from a two-template conformal p p -value. This variant consistently outperforms Uniform aggregation baseline, with relative improvements from 2.1% to 9.2% across all benchmarks. This indicates that calibration effectively differentiates reliable from uncertain rubric judgments even without using template ensembling in the final score. ❸ The benefits of multi-template ensembling and conformal calibration can be synergistically integrated. sections.heading: Varying Rubric Sources.
sections.text: We further evaluate URW across human-audited and LLM-generated rubric sources on RubricBench and ResearchQA. Tables 3 and 4 present the results, with key observations as follows. ❶ URW yields consistent improvements even when LLM-generated rubrics are less effective. Replacing human-audited rubrics with LLM-generated ones lowers absolute accuracy for all methods and benchmarks ( e.g. ,Qwen 3.8 Max Uniform drops from 0.791 0.791 to 0.538 0.538 on RubricBench), indicating that the generated rubrics provide weaker signals for preference judgment. Nevertheless, URW improves over Uniform in all configurations, with relative improvements of 1.6 % 1.6\% – 13.6 % 13.6\% . ❷ URW consistently outperforms uncertainty-aware weighting methods across rubric sources. URW is the best-performing method in every configuration, without source-specific re-tuning. In contrast, the gains of competing methods are not uniformly positive: Sampling Ensemble and SCP fall below Uniform in some generated-rubric settings. These results show that URW’s criterion-level uncertainty weighting provides stronger preference aggregation than alternative uncertainty-aware weighting methods under both human-audited and LLM-generated rubrics.

sections.heading: 4.6 Downstream RLVR Performance (RQ5)
sections.text: In this section, we investigate the downstream RLVR performance of incorporating URW into rubric-based reward aggregation. We construct a training corpus from RubricHub ( Li et al., 2026b ) , sampling 1,000 prompts from each of its Chat and Science domains. We optimize policies with GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) using the VeRL-Rubric framework 3 3 3 https://github.com/DoYangTan/verl-rubric . . We consider Qwen 3 8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and GLM 4 9B ( Glm et al., 2024 ) as policy models, paired with Qwen 3 32B and GLM 4 32B as their respective rubric verifiers. All aggregation methods are trained for an identical budget of 150 150 steps. The trained policies are evaluated zero-shot on Arena-Hard ( Li et al., 2025b ) using win rate (WR) and GPQA-Diamond ( Rein et al., 2024 ) using accuracy (Acc). More implementation details are provided in Appendix C.2 . Tables 5 and 6 present results, with key observations as follows. ❶ All uncertainty-aware weighting methods improve downstream RLVR performance over Uniform aggregation. For example, with Qwen 3 8B as the policy model, Mondrian-SCP improves the Arena-Hard win rate and GPQA-Diamond accuracy over Uniform by 12.81 % 12.81\% and 13.76 % 13.76\% , respectively. This indicates that accounting for criterion-level uncertainty yields more effective reward signals for policy optimization. ❷ URW achieves the best downstream RLVR performance across policy models and benchmarks. URW attains the highest score in all four policy-model–benchmark configurations. For example, with GLM 4 9B as the policy model, URW improves the Arena-Hard win rate from 42.4 42.4 to 48.7 48.7 for the strongest baseline Mondrian-SCP, and the GPQA-Diamond accuracy from 43.4 43.4 to 50.0 50.0 . These results show that continuous uncertainty-aware weighting in URW provides stronger reward aggregation than the competing methods.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we investigated the problem of uncertainty-aware rubric weighting , which aims to account for heterogeneous uncertainty among criterion-level judgments when aggregating rubric-based LLM evaluations. We identified that deterministic black-box verifiers provide no direct verification-confidence signal, causing uniform aggregation to assign equal influence to uncertain and confident judgments. To address this challenge, we proposed Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW) , a training-free and distribution-free framework that ensembles paraphrased judgment templates and calibrates their agreement with split-conformal p p -values to construct continuous criterion-level weights. Theoretically, we demonstrated that URW controls the probability of assigning a spuriously low weight to a correct judgment under exchangeability. Extensive experiments across diverse verifiers and benchmarks confirm that URW improves preference aggregation over competitive baselines and yields more effective rewards for downstream RLVR.

sections.heading: Limitations & Future Work.
sections.text: This work generally has two limitations that warrant future investigation. First, URW’s theoretical guarantee relies on exchangeability between calibration and test triples, which can be strained by distribution shifts during RLVR training. Periodic re-calibration and adaptive inference techniques ( Gibbs and Candes, 2021 ) are promising directions to counteract such shifts. Second, URW quantifies only the uncertainty revealed by a fixed pool of semantics-preserving judgment templates; it does not separately identify other sources of uncertainty, such as intrinsic ambiguity in the rubric or the underlying task. Incorporating complementary uncertainty signals while retaining calibration guarantees is an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: This work lies at the intersection of rubric-based LLM evaluation and uncertainty estimation for LLM judges. The former decomposes open-ended quality into explicit, verifiable criteria, while the latter seeks to characterize when automated judgments should be trusted. URW occupies a distinctive point in this landscape: it converts the cross-template stability of a frozen binary verifier into a split-conformal, criterion-level aggregation weight with a distribution-free validity guarantee.

sections.heading: A.1 Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
sections.text: Rubric-based evaluation provides a transparent alternative to holistic LLM judging by decomposing a response into explicit criteria and verifying them separately. Early checklist-based methods use generated criteria to guide both evaluation and generation ( Cook et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent benchmarks and datasets develop instance-specific, fine-grained rubrics for assessing open-ended outputs ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Recent work further improves rubric construction through self-evolving generation ( Chen et al., 2026b ) and structured meta-rubrics that compile rich evaluation requirements into machine-gradable binary checks ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Rubric judgments have also become a practical source of reward for post-training ( Mu et al., 2024 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Shan and Shao, 2026 ) and, increasingly, for agent improvement in domains without exact verifiers ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These works improve the construction, coverage, or downstream use of rubrics, but commonly aggregate criterion judgments with fixed weights. URW is complementary: it retains the underlying rubric and verifier pipeline while calibrating the reliability of each criterion judgment before aggregation.

sections.heading: A.2 Uncertainty Estimation for LLM Judges
sections.text: A broad line of work studies how to quantify uncertainty in LLM-based evaluation. One line of work uses conformal prediction to provide distribution-free uncertainty at the response level, including rating intervals, consensus intervals, or confidence indicators ( Wagner et al., 2024 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ; Liu, 2026 ) . More generally, split conformal prediction provides finite-sample marginal validity under exchangeability ( Lei et al., 2018 ) , while weighted and adaptive variants extend calibration to settings with covariate or distribution shift ( Tibshirani et al., 2019 ; Gibbs and Candes, 2021 ) . In contrast to using conformal inference to produce a response-level interval, set, or abstention decision, URW evaluates the plausibility of each voted rubric label and directly uses its conformal p p -value as a continuous aggregation weight. Another line of work elicits confidence from decoding-time consistency ( Li et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026 ) or disagreement among heterogeneous judge committees ( Fathullah and Gales, 2025 ) . These approaches require either non-zero-temperature sampling or multiple verifier models. URW instead keeps a single verifier frozen and deterministic, and probes judgment stability through a fixed pool of semantic-preserving templates. A third line of work trains dedicated uncertainty-aware evaluators or calibration probes on top of LLM judges ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Radharapu et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, URW calibrates its criterion-level signal on held-out labeled data without training an additional evaluator. This design makes the uncertainty estimate directly compatible with weighted rubric aggregation.

sections.heading: C.1 Dataset Descriptions
sections.text: In this section, we describe the four categories of data used in our experiments: (1) Pairwise Preference Benchmarks for evaluating rubric aggregation, (2) Calibration Data for constructing the split-conformal reference distribution, (3) RLVR Training Data for policy optimization, and (4) RLVR Evaluation Benchmarks for assessing the resulting policies.

sections.heading: Pairwise Preference Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate URW on five pairwise preference benchmarks. Each instance contains a prompt, two candidate responses ( y A , y B ) (y_{\mathrm{A}},y_{\mathrm{B}}) , and a gold preference label. We apply the same rubric-based scoring protocol to both responses and compare their aggregate scores. RubricBench and ResearchQA provide human-sourced rubrics, whereas rubrics for the remaining benchmarks are generated by RubricARM-8B-Rubric ( Xu et al., 2026c ) . • RubricBench ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/DonJoey/rubricbench : A benchmark of 1,147 1{,}147 response pairs with expert-annotated atomic rubrics. Its examples are designed to expose misleading surface cues that can cause an evaluator to deviate from the human preference. • ResearchQA ( Yifei et al., 2026 ) 5 5 5 https://huggingface.co/datasets/realliyifei/ResearchQA : A collection of 169 169 directional pairs of scholarly long-form answers, accompanied by rubric items mined from survey-style evaluation criteria. • RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025b ) 6 6 6 https://huggingface.co/datasets/THU-KEG/RM-Bench : A benchmark probing sensitivity to subtle content edits and resistance to style bias. Because each instance provides lists of M > 1 M>1 chosen and rejected responses rather than a single pair, we construct 387 387 pairs by matching the m m -th chosen response with the m m -th rejected response for each m m . • RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) 7 7 7 https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/reward-bench : We evaluate on its Chat-Hard subset, which contains 456 456 adversarial chat pairs and is the most challenging subset under the benchmark’s protocol. • RewardBench 2 ( Malik et al., 2026 ) 8 8 8 https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/reward-bench-2 : We use its Precise-IF subset of 480 480 pairs, which focuses on fine-grained instruction-following preferences.

sections.heading: Calibration Data.
sections.text: URW calibrates criterion-level nonconformity scores using RUBRIC-ARROW-Judge-SFT ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) 9 9 9 https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenRubrics/RubricARROW-Judge-SFT , a domain-diverse rubric-annotation corpus. We stratify the corpus by domain and sample 200 200 prompts, producing approximately 2,000 2{,}000 rubric-response-label tuples in 𝒟 cal \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} . The calibration data are disjoint from every evaluation split. This broad coverage is intended to make the exchangeability condition in Assumption B.1 a reasonable approximation; as discussed in Appendix B , the formal guarantee applies when this condition holds.

sections.heading: RLVR Training Data.
sections.text: For downstream RLVR evaluation, we construct the policy-optimization training corpus from RubricHub ( Li et al., 2026b ) 10 10 10 https://huggingface.co/datasets/sojuL/RubricHub_v1 . We exclude prompts with fewer than 4 4 or more than 20 20 rubrics, then randomly sample 1,000 1{,}000 prompts from each of its Chat and Science domains, yielding 2,000 2{,}000 training prompts in total. This mixture exposes policy optimization to both open-ended interaction and knowledge-intensive requests, while retaining a domain structure compatible with rubric-based reward construction. For each prompt, the corresponding rubric set is used to score sampled policy responses; URW then aggregates the criterion-level verifier judgments into the scalar reward used by GRPO. The same training corpus is used for other baselines, so their downstream comparison isolates the effect of the reward-aggregation rule.

sections.heading: RLVR Evaluation Benchmarks.
sections.text: We assess trained policies zero-shot on two held-out benchmarks that cover complementary capabilities. • Arena-Hard ( Li et al., 2025b ) 11 11 11 https://github.com/wsysoft/arena-hard : A benchmark of 500 500 challenging single-turn prompts. It evaluates each policy response by pairwise comparison against the official gpt-4-0314 response; we report win rate. • GPQA-Diamond ( Rein et al., 2024 ) 12 12 12 https://huggingface.co/datasets/fingertap/GPQA-Diamond : A benchmark of 198 198 expert-level, graduate-domain multiple-choice questions; we report accuracy. We deterministically shuffle the four options using a seed derived from each record identifier and a global salt of 42 42 . Together, these benchmarks test whether a reward learned from the Chat and Science training mixture transfers to rigorous scientific reasoning and general instruction following. Neither evaluation benchmark is used to construct the RLVR reward or tune the aggregation method.

sections.heading: C.2 Implementation Details
sections.text: In this section, we provide the implementation details for all experiments. We first present the prompt used by RubricARM-8B-Rubric to generate reference rubrics for benchmarks without human-sourced rubrics. We then describe the fixed verifier-inference and template-ensemble configuration, followed by the baseline hyperparameters and downstream RLVR protocol. URW is training-free: after constructing 𝒟 cal \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} , it only invokes frozen verifiers and performs deterministic aggregation of their binary outputs.

sections.heading: Reference-Rubric Generation Prompt.
sections.text: For RM-Bench, RewardBench, and RewardBench 2, which do not provide human-sourced rubrics, we use RubricARM-8B-Rubric ( Xu et al., 2026c ) to generate a prompt-specific reference rubric set from each original user prompt. The exact system–user prompt is given below. The placeholder {prompt} is replaced with the original user task prompt. The model returns a JSON list of atomic criteria, which we use as the criterion set for scoring both responses in each pair. Prompt C.1: RubricARM-8B-Rubric prompt used to generate reference rubrics. System: You are RubricGenerator. Create prompt-specific rubrics for evaluating responses to one user task. The rubrics must be executable by a separate binary verifier and hard to satisfy through verbosity, boilerplate, or keyword stuffing. Favor orthogonal criteria that test independent quality dimensions and failure modes. User: Create a concise, complete, and orthogonal set of prompt-specific rubrics. Original user task prompt: {prompt} You must return only valid JSON matching this schema: {"rubrics": [ {"rubric_id": "r001", "criterion": "..."} ]} Rules: - Rubrics must be prompt-specific, not generic helpfulness criteria. - Each criterion must be atomic, self-contained, and binary-verifiable. - Keep each criterion under 45 words. - Prefer criteria that distinguish better answers from weaker answers under the prompt. - Generate 5 to 7 rubrics unless the prompt is too narrow for that many independent criteria. - Make the rubrics as orthogonal as possible: each rubric should test a distinct quality dimension or independent failure mode. - Avoid duplicate, overlapping, vague, compound, contradictory, or unverifiable criteria. - Do not split one repeated pattern into multiple near-identical slot checks; use one broader criterion unless each slot is independently essential. - Do not copy long lists, examples, or constraint inventories from the prompt; summarize them compactly in the criterion. - Include both positive requirements and negative-failure guards when useful, but every criterion must still be phrased so that satisfying it is good for the response. - For negative-failure guards, use "The response does not …" or equivalent wording; do not write a criterion where satisfying harmful behavior would add score. - Do not include method-specific weights. - Use rubric ids r001, r002, … in order. - Each criterion should start with "The response". - Return JSON only.

sections.heading: Verifier Inference and Judgment Templates.
sections.text: Unless otherwise noted, we use DeepSeek V4 Pro ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , Qwen 3.8 Max ( Team, 2026 ) , and GLM 5.3 ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) as frozen black-box verifiers. Reference calls use temperature 0 0 , JSON mode, high reasoning effort, and a maximum output length of 32,768 32{,}768 tokens. For each criterion, we query a fixed pool 𝒯 \mathcal{T} of N = 6 \mathrm{N}=6 semantics-preserving judgment templates, reproduced below. The six system–user template pairs are indexed from 0 0 to 5 5 in the evaluation implementation; the placeholders {prompt} , {response} , and {criterion} are replaced with the instance-specific user request, candidate response, and rubric criterion, respectively. Each candidate template was authored by one author and cross-audited by another on 50 50 randomly sampled rubric-response pairs. We discard a template if more than 2 2 of the 50 50 audits identify a semantics-changing behavior, and freeze the resulting pool before running the reported experiments. Prompt C.2: Judgment template pool used for template ensembling. Template 0. System: You are a strict rubric verifier. Given one user prompt, one response, and ONE evaluation criterion, decide whether the response satisfies that criterion. Judge only this local criterion, not overall response quality, and never compare against another response. Mark satisfied=1 only when the response clearly and completely satisfies the criterion; partial satisfaction is 0. Return strict JSON only. User: Original user prompt: {prompt} ; Response to verify: {response} ; Single criterion: {criterion} Verification rules: - Judge only the criterion’s stated local boundary. Do not fail it merely because another part of the overall task is weak or missing. - Preserve exact quantifiers: exactly, at least, at most, only, every, and each are not interchangeable. - If the criterion forbids or says to avoid something, satisfied=1 only when the prohibited condition is absent. - Judge meaning and response evidence, not keyword overlap. - The reason must be one concise final justification. The satisfied bit and reason must agree. Return exactly: {"satisfied": 1, "reason": "short evidence-based reason"} Template 1. System: You are a precise rubric evaluator. You will be given a user prompt, a response, and a single evaluation criterion. Your task is to determine whether the criterion is met. Output satisfied=1 when the criterion is fully met; otherwise output satisfied=0. Respond only with strict JSON. User: User prompt: {prompt} ; Candidate response: {response} ; Evaluation criterion: {criterion} . Guidelines: - Assess only whether the specific criterion above is fulfilled by the response. - Do not penalize for weaknesses outside the scope of this criterion. - Respect exact quantifiers (exactly, at least, at most, only, every, each). - For prohibitive criteria (avoid, must not, never), mark satisfied=1 only when the prohibited element is entirely absent. - Base your judgment on semantic content, not surface-level keyword matching. - Provide a single brief justification that is consistent with the binary verdict. Output format: {"satisfied": 1, "reason": "concise justification"} Template 2. System: You are an impartial criterion checker. Given a prompt, a response, and one rubric criterion, answer whether the response passes that criterion. Return satisfied=1 for pass and satisfied=0 for fail. Output only valid JSON. User: The original request from the user: {prompt} ; The response under evaluation: {response} ; The criterion to check: {criterion} . Instructions: - Does the response satisfy the stated criterion? Focus exclusively on this single criterion, ignoring other aspects of quality. - Quantifiers matter: exactly means exactly, at least means at least, etc. - If the criterion states something should be avoided, the response passes only if that thing is absent. - Evaluate based on meaning and evidence, not keyword presence. - Write a short reason that agrees with your binary decision. Reply with: {"satisfied": 1, "reason": "brief rationale"} Template 3. System: You are a binary rubric judge. Evaluate a single criterion against one response. Output JSON with satisfied (0 or 1) and reason. User: Prompt: {prompt} ; Response: {response} ; Criterion: {criterion} . Decide: does this response fully satisfy the above criterion? - Scope: only this criterion, not overall quality. - Quantifier precision: exactly ≠ \neq at least ≠ \neq at most. - Prohibition: satisfied=1 only if the forbidden element is absent. - Judgment basis: semantic evidence, not keyword overlap. - Output one concise reason aligned with the verdict. {"satisfied": 0, "reason": "..."} Template 4. System: You are a rubric compliance auditor. You receive one user prompt, one response, and one criterion. Determine compliance. Return strict JSON: satisfied=1 for compliant, satisfied=0 for non-compliant. User: ### User Prompt: {prompt} ; ### Response: {response} ; ### Criterion: {criterion} . Task: Determine whether the response is compliant with the criterion above. Rules: 1. Evaluate ONLY this specific criterion in isolation. 2. Exact quantifiers (exactly, at least, at most, only, every, each) must be interpreted literally. 3. For negative criteria (avoid X, must not Y), compliance requires the prohibited element to be entirely absent. 4. Judge by semantic content and evidence, not surface keyword matching. 5. Provide a concise reason consistent with the compliance decision. Output: {"satisfied": 1, "reason": "short evidence-based justification"} Template 5. System: You are a neutral third-party observer asked to verify whether a single evaluation criterion holds for a given response. You must not consider any aspect of quality beyond the stated criterion. Output a JSON object with two fields: satisfied (integer 0 or 1) and reason (string). User: Below is the user’s original request: {prompt} ; Below is the response that was generated: {response} ; The evaluation criterion is: {criterion} . Your task: Determine whether the response meets this criterion. Consider only this criterion and nothing else about the response. Key principles: - Quantifiers are literal: “exactly 3” means precisely 3, not 2 or 4. - Negative requirements (avoid, do not, must not) pass only when the forbidden element is completely absent. - Judge substance and meaning rather than superficial keyword presence. - State a brief reason that directly supports your binary verdict. Respond with exactly: {"satisfied": 1, "reason": "one-sentence justification"}

sections.heading: Baselines and Hyperparameters.
sections.text: All methods use the same verifier outputs whenever their protocols permit. URW directly uses the calibration-score set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} in Eq. ( 4 ) and introduces no tunable hyperparameter. For Sampling Ensemble ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , we independently decode each rubric six times at temperature T = 0.7 \mathrm{T}=0.7 and use its vote ratio as the uncertainty signal. For Beta-Binomial, we use a uniform Beta ⁡ ( 1 , 1 ) \mathrm{Beta}(1,1) prior over each criterion’s satisfaction probability and take the posterior mean as its weight. SCP and Mondrian-SCP use the same template-averaged score v ^ k \hat{v}_{k} as URW, with α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 ; Mondrian-SCP partitions v ^ k \hat{v}_{k} into B = 6 \mathrm{B}=6 bins for bin-wise calibration.

sections.heading: Downstream RLVR Protocol.
sections.text: We optimize Qwen 3 8B and GLM 4 9B policies with GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) using the VeRL-Rubric framework 13 13 13 https://github.com/DoYangTan/verl-rubric . Qwen 3 32B serves as the rubric verifier for Qwen 3 8B, and GLM 4 32B serves as the rubric verifier for GLM 4 9B. For a sampled policy response, the verifier evaluates every criterion under the fixed template pool, and the resulting binary judgments are aggregated with the method-specific rule to form the GRPO reward. Uniform, Mondrian-SCP, and URW therefore share the same policy backbone, verifier family, training prompts, and optimization framework; only their rubric-reward aggregation differs. Each policy is optimized for 150 150 GRPO steps over the 2,000 2{,}000 -prompt training corpus, with an identical step budget across methods. We perform no in-domain fine-tuning on Arena-Hard or GPQA-Diamond. During evaluation, both policies use temperature 1.0 1.0 , with maximum output lengths of 16,384 16{,}384 tokens.

sections.heading: GPQA-Diamond Evaluation.
sections.text: For each question, the policy receives the following zero-shot chain-of-thought prompt, where the four options are the deterministically shuffled choices described above. sections.text: In this subsection, we complement the template-count sensitivity analysis in Section 4.5 with RM-Bench, RewardBench, and RewardBench 2. Figure 4 reports accuracy as the template count N \mathrm{N} varies from 1 1 to 6 6 for the same three verifier profiles; as in the main text, N = 1 \mathrm{N}=1 corresponds to Uniform aggregation. We make two observations. ❶ Multi-template aggregation consistently improves over Uniform aggregation. Across the additional benchmarks and verifier backbones, using more than one template generally yields higher accuracy than the single-template Uniform baseline. This pattern extends the main-text results and shows that the benefit of aggregating cross-template verifier behavior is not restricted to a particular benchmark or model family. ❷ URW is robust to the exact template count. Most performance gains emerge with a small template pool, after which the curves largely plateau or vary only modestly. Although individual trajectories can fluctuate as templates contribute overlapping or complementary judgment signals, the overall pattern indicates that URW does not require delicate tuning of N \mathrm{N} to obtain its benefit. sections.text: In this subsection, we present qualitative case studies illustrating how rubric-reward aggregation translates into downstream policy behavior. We conduct the analysis on GPQA-Diamond. From the responses, we draw two observations. ❶ Policies trained with Uniform aggregation and uncertainty-aware baselines make incorrect final predictions in both cases. All non-URW policies shown in the tables select an incorrect answer on their respective case. These examples suggest that uniformly or heuristically aggregating criterion-level judgments can yield reward signals that do not consistently favor the reasoning patterns required for the correct answer. ❷ Only URW-trained policies produce the correct answer in both cases. In contrast, the URW-trained Qwen 3 8B and GLM 4 9B policies each identify the correct option after providing task-relevant reasoning. While these qualitative examples do not establish a general performance guarantee, they are consistent with the aggregate GPQA-Diamond results in Section 4.6 and illustrate how calibrated criterion-level weighting can support downstream scientific reasoning. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW) , a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal p p -values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment. 1 Introduction Evaluating open-ended outputs of large language models (LLMs) increasingly relies on rubric-based evaluation, in which response quality is decomposed into explicit criteria and assessed by LLM verifiers ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ) . Generally, the verifier renders binary pass or fail judgments on these prompt-specific criteria, which are then aggregated into a response-level score ( Cook et al., 2024 ) . The resulting scores underpin downstream applications such as ranking candidate responses ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) , providing reward signals for reinforcement learning (RL) ( Mu et al., 2024 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Shan and Shao, 2026 ) and verifying agent systems ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026c ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Xu et al., 2026d ) . Consequently, reliable aggregation of rubric judgments is essential for both LLM response evaluation and policy optimization. Despite rapid progress in rubric generation and evolution ( Cook et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , aggregation of rubric judgments heavily relies on uniform weighting. This uniformity reflects a critical limitation: rubric judgments carry no signal of uncertainty. Verifiers output a binary decision per criterion, without any confidence signal that aggregation could use for weighting. However, the difficulty of rendering a reliable judgment varies substantially across criteria ( Song et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . For example, format-level checks are typically clear-cut, while criteria involving tone, helpfulness, or content quality are often inherently subjective and harder to judge ( Pombal et al., 2026 ) . Under uniform aggregation, both types of criteria are collapsed into binary votes and given equal weight. When two responses are otherwise closely matched, an uncertain judgment on one subjective criterion can be enough to invert the overall preference. However, existing work on uncertainty quantification for LLM judges does not fully address the need for per-criterion, uncertainty-aware weighting. One line of work uses conformal prediction to estimate response-level uncertainty, either as a prediction interval over the aggregated rating ( Sheng et al., 2025 ; Liu, 2026 ) or as a confidence flag ( Wagner et al., 2024 ) , characterizing uncertainty in the final rating rather than at the criterion level. Another line of work derives confidence from decoding-time consistency, but requires non-zero-temperature sampling ( Li et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026 ) or heterogeneous verifier committees ( Fathullah and Gales, 2025 ) , both incompatible with common deterministic, single-verifier settings. A third line of work trains dedicated uncertainty modules on top of LLM judges, either by fine-tuning uncertainty-aware evaluators ( Xie et al., 2025 ) or by learning calibration probes ( Radharapu et al., 2026 ) , requiring annotated training data and producing additional output labels rather than a coverage-controlled scalar weight compatible with weighted-sum aggregation. Overall, no existing method provides a training-free, coverage-controlled, per-criterion uncertainty weight that can be applied to any binary-rubric verifier at inference time. To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW) , a training-free framework that quantifies per-criterion uncertainty of any verifier and turns it into a distribution-free aggregation weight. In the offline calibration phase, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from the verifier via a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates, and measures how well this signal aligns with gold labels on a small calibration set. In the online weighting phase, URW converts the soft signal for each new criterion into a split-conformal p p -value, which directly serves as the per-criterion aggregation weight and inherits a distribution-free guarantee: the probability of assigning a spuriously low weight to a correct judgment is provably controlled. Extensive experiments across diverse preference benchmarks and verifier families demonstrate that URW consistently improves both pairwise preference accuracy and downstream RL alignment. Contributions. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows. ❶ We identify an overlooked limitation of rubric-based LLM evaluation: rubric judgments carry no per-criterion uncertainty, so uniform aggregation can let a single unreliable judgment on a closely contested criterion invert the overall preference between two otherwise comparable responses. ❷ We propose URW, a training-free framework for uncertainty-aware rubric weighting. URW couples paraphrase-template ensembling with split-conformal calibration, producing a per-criterion p p -value that serves as an aggregation weight and provably controls the chance of spuriously downweighting a correct judgment. ❸ We conduct comprehensive experiments on five preference benchmarks to evaluate the efficacy of URW, showing that it consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy over diverse baselines and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Rubric-Based Preference Evaluation Rubric-based preference evaluation has recently emerged as an interpretable alternative or complement to conventional reward modeling ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Pan et al., 2026a ; Pan et al., 2026b ) . These weights can be used in place of uniform weights in rubric aggregation. Ideally, they reflect the relative certainty of individual rubric judgments, so that judgments with greater uncertainty exert less influence on the response-level aggregation. However, a deterministic verifier provides only a binary judgment for each criterion and does not directly expose its certainty. Thus, the core problem is to construct w ^ k ​ ( q , y ) \hat{w}_{k}(q,y) from observable verifier behavior that captures uncertainty in individual rubric judgments. 3 Methodology 3.1 Motivation Judgment certainty for rubric criteria is unobservable from the LLM verifier. Existing methods either estimate response-wise uncertainty rather than per criterion ( Sheng et al., 2025 ; Liu, 2026 ; Wagner et al., 2024 ) , rely on higher-temperature sampling or verifier committees that depart from the deterministic reference decoding ( Li et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Fathullah and Gales, 2025 ) , or train dedicated modules that require annotated data and emit auxiliary labels instead of an criterion-level weight ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Radharapu et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate URW on five pairwise preference benchmarks across different domains, including RubricBench ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , ResearchQA ( Yifei et al., 2026 ) , RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) , and RewardBench 2 ( Malik et al., 2026 ) . For RewardBench and RewardBench 2, we adopt their most challenging subsets, namely Chat-Hard and Precise-IF, respectively. Each benchmark supplies a response pair ( y A , y B ) (y_{\mathrm{A}},y_{\mathrm{B}}) per prompt together with a gold human preference label. For RM-Bench, whose instances list multiple chosen and rejected responses, we form pairs by diagonal matching. RubricBench and ResearchQA come with human-sourced rubrics, whereas for the remaining benchmarks we generate rubrics with RubricARM-8B-Rubric ( Xu et al., 2026c ) . For calibration in URW, we draw from the domain-diverse RUBRIC-ARROW-Judge-SFT rubric-annotation corpus ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , whose broad domain coverage supports the exchangeability our method assumes. We stratify by domain and sample 200 200 prompts, yielding about 2 2 k rubric-level annotations. The calibration set never intersects any evaluation split. Detailed dataset statistics and configurations are provided in Appendix C.1 . Baselines. We benchmark URW against a naive reference and a suite of uncertainty-aware weighting baselines, including Uniform ( w k = 1 / K w_{k}=1/\mathrm{K} ), the signal-free floor that weights all criteria equally; Beta-Binomial , a Bayesian method that treats the multi-template judgments as binomial observations under a Beta prior and derives the weight from the resulting posterior; Sampling Ensemble ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , which draws multiple high-temperature decodings per criterion and weights by their vote ratio; and SCP , a distribution-free method that calibrates the same multi-template soft score v ^ \hat{v} and hard-abstains via a global conformal quantile, together with its variant Mondrian-SCP that instead calibrates a separate quantile within each bin of v ^ \hat{v} . These results show that continuous uncertainty-aware weighting in URW provides stronger reward aggregation than the competing methods. 5 Conclusion In this work, we investigated the problem of uncertainty-aware rubric weighting , which aims to account for heterogeneous uncertainty among criterion-level judgments when aggregating rubric-based LLM evaluations. We identified that deterministic black-box verifiers provide no direct verification-confidence signal, causing uniform aggregation to assign equal influence to uncertain and confident judgments. To address this challenge, we proposed Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW) , a training-free and distribution-free framework that ensembles paraphrased judgment templates and calibrates their agreement with split-conformal p p -values to construct continuous criterion-level weights. Theoretically, we demonstrated that URW controls the probability of assigning a spuriously low weight to a correct judgment under exchangeability. Extensive experiments across diverse verifiers and benchmarks confirm that URW improves preference aggregation over competitive baselines and yields more effective rewards for downstream RLVR. Limitations & Future Work. This work generally has two limitations that warrant future investigation. First, URW’s theoretical guarantee relies on exchangeability between calibration and test triples, which can be strained by distribution shifts during RLVR training. Periodic re-calibration and adaptive inference techniques ( Gibbs and Candes, 2021 ) are promising directions to counteract such shifts. Second, URW quantifies only the uncertainty revealed by a fixed pool of semantics-preserving judgment templates; it does not separately identify other sources of uncertainty, such as intrinsic ambiguity in the rubric or the underlying task. Incorporating complementary uncertainty signals while retaining calibration guarantees is an important direction for future work. References Arora et al. (2025) R. K. Arora, J. Wei, R. S. Hicks, P. Cited by: 1st item , §4.1 . Appendix A Related Work This work lies at the intersection of rubric-based LLM evaluation and uncertainty estimation for LLM judges. The former decomposes open-ended quality into explicit, verifiable criteria, while the latter seeks to characterize when automated judgments should be trusted. URW occupies a distinctive point in this landscape: it converts the cross-template stability of a frozen binary verifier into a split-conformal, criterion-level aggregation weight with a distribution-free validity guarantee. A.1 Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation Rubric-based evaluation provides a transparent alternative to holistic LLM judging by decomposing a response into explicit criteria and verifying them separately. Early checklist-based methods use generated criteria to guide both evaluation and generation ( Cook et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent benchmarks and datasets develop instance-specific, fine-grained rubrics for assessing open-ended outputs ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Recent work further improves rubric construction through self-evolving generation ( Chen et al., 2026b ) and structured meta-rubrics that compile rich evaluation requirements into machine-gradable binary checks ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Rubric judgments have also become a practical source of reward for post-training ( Mu et al., 2024 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Shan and Shao, 2026 ) and, increasingly, for agent improvement in domains without exact verifiers ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These works improve the construction, coverage, or downstream use of rubrics, but commonly aggregate criterion judgments with fixed weights. URW is complementary: it retains the underlying rubric and verifier pipeline while calibrating the reliability of each criterion judgment before aggregation. A.2 Uncertainty Estimation for LLM Judges A broad line of work studies how to quantify uncertainty in LLM-based evaluation. One line of work uses conformal prediction to provide distribution-free uncertainty at the response level, including rating intervals, consensus intervals, or confidence indicators ( Wagner et al., 2024 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ; Liu, 2026 ) . More generally, split conformal prediction provides finite-sample marginal validity under exchangeability ( Lei et al., 2018 ) , while weighted and adaptive variants extend calibration to settings with covariate or distribution shift ( Tibshirani et al., 2019 ; Gibbs and Candes, 2021 ) . In contrast to using conformal inference to produce a response-level interval, set, or abstention decision, URW evaluates the plausibility of each voted rubric label and directly uses its conformal p p -value as a continuous aggregation weight. Another line of work elicits confidence from decoding-time consistency ( Li et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026 ) or disagreement among heterogeneous judge committees ( Fathullah and Gales, 2025 ) . These approaches require either non-zero-temperature sampling or multiple verifier models. URW instead keeps a single verifier frozen and deterministic, and probes judgment stability through a fixed pool of semantic-preserving templates. A third line of work trains dedicated uncertainty-aware evaluators or calibration probes on top of LLM judges ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Radharapu et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, URW calibrates its criterion-level signal on held-out labeled data without training an additional evaluator. This design makes the uncertainty estimate directly compatible with weighted rubric aggregation.
